title: T3 — Terraform state
bodyMarkdown:
## Terraform state

Exam group **6**. Group 2 explained why Terraform keeps state and that by default it is a local `terraform.tfstate` file; group 3 gave the command loop that reads and writes it. This group covers where that state lives (backends), how two writers are kept from colliding (locking), how a remote backend is configured, and how to keep state truthful when the real world or your code changes (drift, import, move, remove).

### tf.004.6a — Describe the local backend

A backend decides where state is stored and how operations run. "Terraform uses a backend called local by default," and the local backend "stores state on the local filesystem, locks that state using system APIs, and performs operations locally." Do not confuse the backend with the state file: the backend is the mechanism, and `terraform.tfstate` is the data it keeps.

You do not need a `backend` block to use it. The docs describe configurations that "default to the local backend by not specifying a backend at all." You only write `backend "local" { ... }` to change its settings: `path` is optional and defaults to `terraform.tfstate` relative to the root module, and `workspace_dir` sets the path for non-default workspaces. A workspace is one named state for a configuration: some backends support "multiple named workspaces, allowing multiple states to be associated with a single configuration," and "Terraform starts with a single, default workspace named default that you cannot delete." Terraform also keeps "a backup of the previous state in terraform.tfstate.backup" next to the state file.

What the local backend lacks is sharing. Storing state locally "limits the ability to collaborate with others, and risks losing workspace state if the local state file is lost." With a local file, "each user must make sure they always have the latest state data before running Terraform," and must also make sure nobody else runs Terraform at the same time. The local backend does lock the file, but the file still sits on one machine, so a team needs a remote backend (6c) and a backend that supports locking (6b).

Three command-line options exist only for this backend: `-state`, `-state-out` and `-backup`. The docs call them "legacy features that we've preserved for backward compatibility but that we no longer recommend." They "have no effect for configurations that have a different backend type selected." The recommended replacement is to "select a different backend which supports remote state."

You can also go back to local. If you remove the backend block and reinitialize, "Terraform also prompts you to migrate the state to the default local backend."

The discriminator: no `backend` block means the local backend and a `terraform.tfstate` file on your own disk; that gives you automatic locking on that machine but no shared copy for teammates and no protection if the file is lost.

**Exam tip:** "no backend block, state in `terraform.tfstate` beside the configuration" is the local backend; "teammates need the latest state and the laptop's file can be lost" is what it lacks; "`-state`, `-state-out` or `-backup`" are legacy local-only options that do nothing under another backend.

### tf.004.6b — Describe state locking

"If supported by your backend, Terraform will lock your state for all operations that could write state." The purpose is to stop a second run from acquiring the lock "and potentially corrupting your state." Three points are easy to mix up.

First, locking is automatic but backend-dependent. "State locking happens automatically on all operations that could write state," with no message from Terraform, and "If state locking fails, Terraform does not continue." But "Not all backends support locking," so read each backend's page. HCP Terraform (HashiCorp's hosted service) "supports an even stronger locking concept" by "queuing Terraform operations in a central location."

Second, two flags change locking behavior. `-lock-timeout=<duration>` sets how long Terraform waits to acquire a lock; its default is "0s (zero seconds), which causes immediate failure if the lock is already held by another process." So a plain run that meets a held lock fails at once rather than waiting. `-lock=false` is different: "You can disable state locking for most commands with the -lock=false flag, but we do not recommend it." The state-modifying commands warn that this is "dangerous if others might concurrently run commands against the same workspace." Use a timeout when you expect contention; do not turn locking off to get past it.

Third, `terraform force-unlock LOCK_ID` is for a stuck lock, not a busy one. "Force unlock should only be used to unlock your own lock in the situation where automatic unlocking failed." If you unlock while a colleague is running, "it could cause multiple writers." It requires the lock ID: "the force-unlock command requires a unique lock ID," which Terraform prints if unlocking fails. It "does not modify your infrastructure," and it does not help with the local backend: "Local state files cannot be unlocked by another process."

Amazon S3 is the common exam backend, so know its exact status. "State locking is an opt-in feature of the S3 backend." "Locking can be enabled via S3 or DynamoDB." S3 locking is turned on with `use_lockfile`, which is optional and "Defaults to false," so an S3 backend with no locking arguments does not lock. DynamoDB locking is the older method: "DynamoDB-based locking is deprecated and will be removed in a future minor version." It uses `dynamodb_table`, and "The table must have a partition key named LockID with a type of String." To ease migration, "the S3 and DynamoDB arguments can be configured simultaneously." With `use_lockfile`, the IAM permissions "s3:GetObject, s3:PutObject, and s3:DeleteObject are required on the lock file," which is separate from the state object itself.

The discriminator: locking prevents concurrent writes and is automatic only where the backend supports it; `-lock-timeout` waits, `-lock=false` skips the protection, and `force-unlock` clears a lock you own after a failure.

**Exam tip:** "two people applied at once and the state was corrupted" is a missing or disabled lock; "run failed immediately because someone else holds the lock" is the default `-lock-timeout` of 0s; "S3 backend with no DynamoDB table that still locks" is `use_lockfile = true`; "stuck lock after a crash, you have the lock ID" is `force-unlock`, never against someone else's live lock.

### tf.004.6c — Configure remote state using the backend block

With remote state, Terraform "writes the state data to a remote data store, which can then be shared between all members of a team." It "is implemented by a backend or by HCP Terraform." To configure a backend, "add a nested backend block within the top-level terraform block." The block label is the backend type, such as `s3`, and the arguments are specific to that type. The S3 backend page opens with "Stores the state as a given key in a given bucket on Amazon S3." "You cannot load additional backends as plugins," and the type must exist in your Terraform version.

The block has hard limits:

- "A configuration can only provide one backend block."
- "A backend block cannot refer to named values (like input variables, locals, or data source attributes)." So `bucket = var.bucket_name` inside it is not allowed.
- A backend block and a `cloud` block cannot coexist: "If your configuration includes a cloud block, it cannot include a backend block."

`backend` and `cloud` are two ways to store remote state. Use the `cloud` block to connect to HCP Terraform or Terraform Enterprise: "Do not configure a backend when connecting your configuration to workspaces in HCP Terraform or Terraform Enterprise," because those systems "automatically manage state in the workspaces associated with your configuration." The `cloud` block follows the same limit as `backend`: "The cloud block cannot refer to named values, such as input variables, locals, or data source attributes." And "You can only provide one cloud block per configuration."

Because backend blocks cannot use variables, values that differ per environment or that are secret go in a partial configuration. "When some or all of the arguments are omitted, we call this a partial configuration," and "the remaining configuration arguments must be provided as part of the initialization process." You supply them in three ways: a file ("use the -backend-config=PATH option when running terraform init"), key/value pairs ("use the -backend-config="KEY=VALUE" option"), or interactively when Terraform asks. Terraform still needs the type: "an empty backend configuration is specified in one of the root Terraform configuration files, to specify the backend type." If a value is given in several places, "any command-line options override the settings in the main configuration," and later options override earlier ones.

Credentials need care. "We recommend using environment variables to supply credentials and other sensitive data." If you hardcode values or use `-backend-config`, "Terraform will include these values in both the .terraform subdirectory and in plan files." The `.terraform/terraform.tfstate` file holds the backend configuration, not your infrastructure state, and "Do not check this directory into Git, as it may contain sensitive credentials for your remote backend."

Changing a backend needs another init: "When you change a backend's configuration, you must run terraform init again." Terraform detects the change and asks about migrating state, and "If you're just reconfiguring the same backend, Terraform will still ask if you want to migrate your state." The two init options differ: "The -migrate-state option will attempt to copy existing state to the new backend," while "The -reconfigure option disregards any existing configuration, preventing migration of any existing state." The docs say "Either -reconfigure or -migrate-state must be supplied to update the backend configuration" when re-running init on an already-initialized backend. `-force-copy` "suppresses these prompts" and "also automatically enables the -migrate-state option." Before migrating, "we strongly recommend manually backing up your state by copying your terraform.tfstate file to another location."

The discriminator: `backend` is for remote backends you configure yourself and cannot use variables; `cloud` is for HCP Terraform workspaces, and the two are mutually exclusive; `-migrate-state` moves existing state to the new location, while `-reconfigure` abandons the old configuration and does not move it.

**Exam tip:** "backend block with a variable fails" is the named-values limit, solved by `-backend-config` and a partial configuration; "switched to a new bucket and wants the existing state copied" is `init -migrate-state`; "ignore the old backend settings without copying state" is `init -reconfigure`; "block that connects to HCP Terraform workspaces" is `cloud`, never alongside `backend`.

### tf.004.6d — Manage resource drift and Terraform state

#### Drift and refresh-only

Drift is state falling out of sync with the real infrastructure after someone changes it by hand. The docs say you "should not make manual changes to resources controlled by Terraform," because the state file will be out of sync, or "drift," from the real infrastructure. By default, "Terraform compares your state file to real infrastructure whenever you invoke terraform plan or terraform apply," so a normal run after a manual change would try to put things back: "without the -refresh-only flag now, Terraform would attempt to revert your manual changes."

Group 3 (3d) introduced `-refresh-only`; here is how it handles drift. It records drift instead of reverting it. `terraform plan -refresh-only` creates a plan whose goal is to "update the Terraform state and any root module output values to match changes made to remote objects outside of Terraform." `terraform apply -refresh-only` is how you accept it: "apply this plan to record the updated values in the Terraform state without changing any remote objects." Either way "A refresh-only operation does not attempt to modify your infrastructure to match your Terraform configuration." Version floor: "The -refresh-only option is available only in Terraform v0.15.4 and later." The older `terraform refresh` command "is deprecated" and "is effectively an alias for the following command: terraform apply -refresh-only -auto-approve," so it overwrites state with no review. If you want the real object back to the configuration, run a normal plan and apply instead.

#### Importing

Bringing an existing object under management is an import, and there are two forms. The `import` block: "Importing unmanaged resources to your workspace requires an import block that specifies the unique infrastructure resource ID to import," with `to` for the address and `id` for the provider's ID. You also "must create a destination resource block that matches the address declared in the import block," because "you must define a resource block for any resource in state to prevent Terraform from destroying it." You run `terraform plan` to preview and `terraform apply` to import. A plan option, `-generate-config-out=PATH`, can write the resource block for you; the plan page labels it experimental, and the target file must not already exist.

The CLI form is the `terraform import ADDRESS ID` command: it will "find the existing resource from ID and import it into your Terraform state at the given ADDRESS." In the docs' own walkthrough of the command, you first "add the resource definition to your configuration" and then run it. The docs steer you to the block: "Instead of manually importing resources, you can add the import block to your Terraform configurations," and configuration-driven import "lets you import multiple resources at once, review the import in your plan-and-apply workflow." That needs Terraform 1.5 or later: "Terraform 1.5+ supports configuration-driven import." With either form, be careful to "import each remote object to only one Terraform resource address."

#### Renaming and forgetting

Renaming and removing are the other state edits, and again there are configuration blocks and CLI commands.

- A `moved` block changes an address without destroying anything: "You can use a moved block to update a resource address without destroying it." Without it, Terraform "interprets a change as an instruction to destroy the existing resource and create a new resource at the new address." Moved blocks need Terraform 1.1 or later ("Terraform v1.1 and later is required to use moved blocks"); the same page says "Instead, use the terraform state mv CLI command." `terraform state mv` is the CLI version: it "changes bindings in Terraform state so that existing remote objects bind to new resource instances," and you can only move "to a new address with the same resource type." The reason to prefer the block is visibility. A `moved` block lives in the configuration and "Terraform includes the update to the resource address in the next execution plan," and chained blocks can "document the full change history." With `state mv` used for a refactor, the docs tell you to "communicate carefully with your coworkers" so that "nobody makes any other changes between your configuration change and your terraform state mv command." The refactor page also calls moving resources between state files with it a legacy approach: "This is a legacy command."
- A `removed` block takes a resource out of state. Its configuration model lists the `lifecycle` block as "required," and "For removed blocks, the only supported lifecycle argument is destroy." Know the default: "By default, Terraform removes the resource from state and destroys the actual resource." To forget it without destroying it, "Set destroy to false to remove the resource from state without destroying the actual resource." In configuration that is `removed { from = <address> lifecycle { destroy = false } }`. The reference page's opening line says the block removes a resource from state "without changing the underlying infrastructure," but its lifecycle section controls destroying with `destroy`, so always write the `lifecycle` block and set `destroy` explicitly. The remove-and-import workflow with these blocks requires "Terraform version 1.7 or newer." `terraform state rm` "removes the binding to an existing remote object without first destroying it," and a later plan proposes creating a new object for each forgotten instance that is still in the configuration. The docs say "we recommend using the removed block instead" because "the removed block lets you preview the results of the operation."

#### Inspecting state

`terraform state list` "lists resources within a Terraform state," and `terraform state show` "shows the attributes of a single resource in the Terraform state." `state list` is read-only and writes no backup. Do not edit the state file by hand: "Terraform stores your workspaces state as a JSON text file. Do not directly edit this file." Use the state commands, which exist "to modify the Terraform state instead modifying the state directly." Every state-modifying subcommand writes a backup: "Terraform forces every state modification command to write a backup file." Terraform "expects a one-to-one mapping between configured resource instances and remote objects," so if you add or remove bindings by importing or with `state rm`, you must keep that one-to-one rule true yourself.

#### Putting it together

The discriminator: refresh-only changes only state to match reality; import adds an existing object to state; `moved` and `state mv` rename an address; `removed` and `state rm` stop managing an object, and only `removed` with `lifecycle { destroy = false }` says explicitly that the real object stays.

**Exam tip:** "someone changed a resource in the console and you want state to match, without touching infrastructure" is `plan` or `apply -refresh-only`; "bring an unmanaged object under Terraform with a plan preview" is an `import` block (1.5 or later); "rename a resource block without destroying the object" is a `moved` block; "stop managing a resource but keep it running" is a `removed` block with `lifecycle { destroy = false }` or `terraform state rm` (the docs give Terraform 1.7 or newer for the remove-and-import workflow); "open the state JSON and fix it" is the wrong answer.

### Warnings

- Do not run `terraform apply` or `terraform destroy` against real cloud credentials in this workbook, and never call `ExecuteTerraformCommand` or `ExecuteTerragruntCommand` from this workbook's tools.
- State can contain secrets in plain text (group 4, section 4h covers how secret values reach state), and "state data contains extremely sensitive information." Never commit a state file or the `.terraform` directory to version control: storing state in a version control system "can result in data loss or exposure of secrets stored in the state file."
- Do not use `-lock=false` or `force-unlock` to get around a lock held by a run that is still working; only clear your own lock after automatic unlocking failed.
- Do not apply a refresh-only plan, `terraform state rm`, `terraform state mv` or a `removed` block without reading what it will change first, and back up the state before migrating a backend.
